sentences.text: The genus Majungasaurus contains only one species, Majungasaurus crenatissimus, and was formally named by Lavocat in 1955 after previously being known as Majungatholus.
This dinosaur is distinguished by a wider skull featuring rough, thickened bone on the snout top and a single rounded horn on the skull roof.
Its most distinctive feature is the cranial ornamentation, which includes swollen, fused nasal bones and a frontal horn.
Majungasaurus was a medium-sized theropod reaching lengths between 5.6 and 7.0 meters and weighing between 750 and 1100 kilograms.
Fossil evidence confirms that this apex predator fed on the sauropod Rapetosaurus, leaving distinct tooth marks on its bones.
Majungasaurus is the only dinosaur for which there is direct evidence of cannibalism.
It appears to be more closely related to Indian abelisaurids than to those from South America or Africa.
Fossils were first found in 1896 by Charles Depéret in northwestern Madagascar, though they were initially misidentified as Megalosaurus.
All known fossils come from the Maevarano Formation, where 25 recorded occurrences of the species have been found.
It was a bipedal dinosaur with a long tail that balanced its head and torso, positioning its center of gravity over its hips.
Researchers suggest it used a bite-and-hold feeding strategy similar to modern cats, relying on a short, broad snout to grip prey rather than slicing it.
Pneumatic foramina in its vertebrae and ribs suggest it had an avian-style respiratory system where inhaled and exhaled air were not mixed.
CT scans of the complete skull allowed a rough reconstruction of its brain, which was very small relative to body size and had a conservative structure closer to modern crocodilians than to birds.
Majungasaurus was among the slowest-growing theropod dinosaurs.
Unlike tyrannosaurids which often show facial bite wounds, no wounds were found on any Majungasaurus skull elements.
Throughout its life, the skull, specifically the jugal, postorbital, and quadratojugal bones, became taller and more robust.
Researchers suggest that the unique skull shape indicates distinct hunting behaviors compared to other theropods.
A 2013 cladogram by Tortosa et al. places Majungasaurus in the new subfamily Majungasaurinae.
Majungasaurus lived in Madagascar between 70 and 66 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Period.
It was the largest carnivore and likely the dominant land predator in its ecosystem, primarily hunting sauropods like Rapetosaurus.
Researchers debated whether the skull fragment originally named Majungatholus atopus belonged to Majungasaurus crenatissimus, initially judging the type dentary too fragmentary to link them.
Researchers suggest the skull horns and crests likely played a role in intraspecific competition, though their exact function remains unknown.

Recent analyses place Majungasaurus in a clade with Indian genera Rajasaurus and Indosaurus, excluding South American and African abelisaurids, suggesting separate clades in western and eastern Gondwana.
